sense: of a newspaper, magazine or book

terms.gloss: editor (of a newspaper, magazine, book); a woman is redāctrīx
evidence: Traupman 308: redāctor prīnceps, editor in chief
terms.comment: A modern coinage from redigō, to bring into order. The long ā by Lachmann’s law, as in āctus.

terms.gloss: a corrector; one who edits a text
evidence: Cic. Balb. 20: corrector atque ēmendātor nostrae cīvitātis (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Classically anyone who corrects or improves something, a state as much as a text; fits the editor who prepares or corrects a text (ēmendāre, Morgan–Owens), not the editor who runs a paper.
Modern, after ēdere, to publish (librum ēdere, Cic.). Classically the word means only “that which brings forth” (Lucan 2.423) and, late, a giver of games (Lewis & Short).

phrases.english: Send this article to the editor.

redactor.html: From redāctus, redigō (agō, āctus): Lachmann’s law. Traupman 308 prints redāctor.

sources: Lewis & Short: emendator · Lewis & Short: editor · Lewis & Short: redigo

John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 308, checked against the searchable text of the book (11 November 2026). Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. edit (prepare a text for publication).
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j); they have not been checked against a modern edition.
